title: Decision Trees
interviewAnswer: Decision trees recursively split the feature space to make child nodes purer. They capture nonlinear interactions and require little preprocessing, but deep trees overfit easily.
why: Decision trees introduce recursive partitioning, impurity measures, overfitting and the foundation for random forests and gradient boosting.
intuition: A tree repeatedly asks simple questions that split the data into purer groups. Each path from root to leaf is an interpretable set of rules.
deepDive: For classification, splits often maximize impurity reduction using Gini or entropy; regression trees reduce squared/absolute error. Trees naturally model nonlinear interactions and mixed scales but are high variance: a small data change can alter structure. Depth, minimum samples and pruning regularize them. Greedy split selection is local, not globally optimal.
math:
Gini = 1-Σ_k p_k²
Entropy = -Σ_k p_k log p_k
Split gain = parent impurity - weighted child impurities
workedExample: A failure classifier might first split on load, then material type, then temperature. The interactions are learned without manually creating load×material features.
commonMistakes: Assuming deeper trees are always better.
Ignoring class imbalance or leakage because trees handle preprocessing well.
production: Tree models are strong tabular baselines. Validate input ranges/categories and monitor feature distributions because splits can behave unexpectedly outside training support.
